title: TC0-08578
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They appeal the decision of the Refugee Protection Division ("RPD") dated March 10, 2020, whereby the RPD found that they were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection pursuant to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 ("IRPA").
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Principal Appellant"), his spouse XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Associate Appellant") and their children, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX ("Minor Appellants") are citizens of Nigeria. They appeal the decision of the Refugee Protection Division ("RPD") dated March 10, 2020, whereby the RPD found that they were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection pursuant to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 ("IRPA"). The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division ("RAD") to set aside the RPD decision and to find that they are Convention refuges and/or persons in need of protection pursuant to the IRPA.
The Appellants have tendered no new evidence under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, but have requested an oral hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.2
The Principal Appellant has been appointed designated representative for the Minor Appellants.

I hereby confirm the RPD decision that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees under section 96 of the IRPA, nor are they persons in need of protection within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. Accordingly, this appeal is dismissed.

The Principal Appellant claims to be a XXXX employed by the XXXX XXXX XXXX in Nigeria where he had been assigned to a XXXX XXXX in Ado Ekiti. In August 2018, his supervisor assigned him a file regarding a loan which had gone into default. He claims that in the course of the investigation, he discovered that a group of five individuals, the agents of persecution, had participated in a fraudulent scheme by which a loan was advanced by the bank to them who then split the proceeds of the loan.

The Principal Appellant alleges that one of the agents of persecution is a banker, another is a highly situated state politician, two others are politically connected individuals who have run unsuccessfully for office and the fifth is a government official who has been described as the president of the Ado Ekiti Primary Healthcare Staff Cooperative Multipurpose Society ("Cooperative Society") which is the agency to which the loan was granted.

The Principal Appellant claims that following the submission of his report, the bank contacted these individuals to invite them to a meeting to discuss the status of the loan. He submitted a comprehensive report to his immediate supervisor, as well as the "zonal" manager. At some point following submission of this report, he began to receive threatening phone calls and in October 2018, he claims that his home was broken into by three individuals who tied he and his family up, slapped him and stole their cellphones. The Appellants have also reported allegations of attempted kidnap and being shot at as part of their claim. This persecutory conduct caused the Appellants to move within Nigeria twice, but they claim that the agents of persecution were able to track them down. They obtained a travel visa to the United States of America ("USA") and departed Nigeria on XXXX XXXX, 2018, where they remained until XXXX XXXX, 2018, at which time they made their way to Canada, where they commenced a claim for refugee protection.

My role is to review the RPD decision on a standard of correctness after having conducted an independent examination of the evidence.3 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard or documentary evidence tendered at the hearing which may, in certain cases, allow me to defer to RPD findings. I do not believe the RPD enjoyed any such meaningful advantage in this matter and all evidence from the RPD hearing has been taken into consideration in arriving at my decision.

The RPD found that the determinative issue was credibility and that the Appellants had failed to meet their burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that they had been targeted by the agents of persecution and that they were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

On appeal, the Appellants argue as follows: (i) the failure of the RPD to produce a complete record of the hearing constitutes a breach of natural justice by denying the Appellants the opportunity to properly prepare and argue their appeal; (ii) the RPD erred by failing to meaningfully engage with and misapprehending the evidence before it when making credibility findings; (iii) the RPD erred by making a hidden plausibility finding; and (iv) under the circumstances, an oral hearing should be held. For reasons which follow, I am not persuaded by counsel's argument with respect to items (i), (ii) and (iv) above. I agree that, with respect to item (iii), the RPD erred in making the impugned implausibility finding but, as set out below, I consider that such finding was not determinative of the issues, nor does it affect the outcome of my decision. Request for an oral hearing is denied

The Appellants argue that an oral hearing should be held in order to address any outstanding credibility concerns surrounding any of the Appellants' evidence.4 In support of this proposition, they cite subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

When read together, subsections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new evidence admitted in accordance with the provisions of subsection 110(4), in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD decision and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

The Appellants have submitted no new evidence in support of their appeal. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing in their appeal, and their application for an oral hearing is denied. No denial of natural justice regarding RPD record

The Appellants argue that the RPD has failed to produce a complete record of the refugee proceeding which constitutes a breach of natural justice. They allege that portions of the hearing audio recording are completely inaudible and the recording as a whole is not comprehensible. As a result, they claim that the inadequate record has created a serious possibility that the Appellants have been denied procedural fairness in pursuing their appeal.

I am not persuaded by this argument. From the outset and for purpose of clarity, I must highlight the fact that there are, in fact, two versions of the transcript at play. Counsel submitted one (unofficial) version with the Appellants' Record, whereas I have been provided with an official transcript prepared by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) from the same RPD audio recording of the proceeding as provided to counsel. Having reviewed the IRB transcript at some length, I note that there is from time to time (as is frequently the case when dealing with transcripts) a notation that a comment or a word was uttered which is shown as "inaudible." I have not undertaken a "side by side" comparison of the two versions of the transcript but have considered several examples provided by counsel in the memorandum and have listened to the audio recording. I might add that it did not occur (at least on the IRB transcript) with respect to exchanges of any great length; it was generally with respect to a single word or two. However, that occurred on a relatively infrequent basis and I was able to follow along with the testimony by considering the line of inquiry and taking into context the question posed, as well as the response given. Despite what I would describe as a minor inconvenience with respect to the occasional missing word, I found no difficulty in comprehending the evidence, was not hampered by the occasional missing word and, in spite of it, was able to give the Appellants' testimony full consideration.

Similarly, with respect to the specific instances referenced by the Appellants, I note that the Appellants memorandum cites another exchange as being illustrative of the transcription problems which form the basis of their argument.5 I contrast this argument with the following excerpt from the IRB transcript: The fraud was committed by the cooperative society that I mentioned in the report. I mentioned the name of the cooperative society. I said - where I mentioned Mrs. XXXX XXXX, the president of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX the account used to populate the form.6 Though counsel's transcript features breaks in the Principal Appellant's response7, the above response appearing in the IRB transcript is a complete and comprehensive response to the question put to the Principal Appellant by the RPD member. In order to satisfy myself as to the accuracy of the IRB transcript, I have listened to the exchanges listed herein and have confirmed them to be accurately reported by the IRB transcript.

Immediately below this excerpt are further statements that appear incomplete in counsel's transcript yet, once again, the IRB transcript is complete.8 Again, the excerpt referenced by counsel9 represents another example where counsel's transcript is incomplete, yet the IRB transcript provides what appears to be a complete version of the Principal Appellant's response which reads as follows: Okay. Let me explain. When the Primary Healthcare process (inaudible), when they took the loan rider, I discovered in my investigation that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, they all took money from the cooperative society, from the loan that the cooperative society took from the branch and from the bank.10

Although counsel's transcript again shows gaps in the Principal Appellant's testimony at this stage of the proceeding, the IRB transcript provides a full response to the question posed by the RPD member. Given the fact that the same hearing audio recording would have been used to prepare both transcript versions, not to mention the fact that I have listened to relevant portions of the audio recording, I am led to believe that it is not a problem with the audio recording of the proceeding but, perhaps, an issue with the equipment used by the transcriptionist who prepared counsel's transcript. Once again, I base this upon my having listened to the relevant sections of the RPD hearing audio recording, which I found to be clear and, apart from the occasional inaudible word, easily followed. It is also worthy of note that it is IRB/RAD policy to provide a copy of the IRB transcript to counsel following a RAD decision in which an official IRB transcript is referenced.

Having highlighted the differences between the two versions of the transcripts and being fully confident that the RPD hearing audio recording is clear; I find I have not suffered anything other than minor inconvenience in conducting my independent assessment of this matter. As I have been able to fully and fairly conduct such assessment, I find that there has been no denial of natural justice occasioned by the RPD hearing tape. Credibility issues

The determinative issue for the RPD was credibility.11 Once again, in conducting my own independent assessment of this matter, I have reviewed the IRB transcript at length, as well as portions of the transcript supplied by counsel and the RPD hearing audio recording, where necessary. I have noted that the IRB transcript is much more reliable than the Appellants' unofficial version as there are relatively few instances where an inaudible response was recorded. When this happened, it was generally limited to one word which did not hinder my ability to follow the testimony. I note that, for the most part, the testimony was in proper context signalling to me that the RPD questions were understood and also that the Principal Appellant quite regularly asked for clarification of questions which requests the RPD unfailingly obliged. The Principal Appellant testified in English and I noted that he was quite proficient in the language and that there were no instances where he (who gave the bulk of testimony on behalf of the Appellants) showed any signs of memory issues associated with the allegations or the aftermath of the alleged persecutory conduct.

Credibility remains the determinative issue for purpose of this appeal. The starting point of any credibility assessment lies with the presumption of truthfulness;12 this presumption - sometimes referred to as the Maldonado presumption - holds that when a refugee claimant swears certain facts to be true, they are presumed truthful unless there be reason to doubt their veracity. The presumption is always rebuttable and may be displaced by an accumulation of contradictions, inconsistencies or omissions or where the documentary evidence fails to mention what one ordinarily might expect it to mention. A refugee claimant's personal credibility and the credibility of the claim must be assessed by the decision-maker and, in both cases, if found wanting, may compromise the success of the claim.

With respect to the credibility issue, the Appellants specifically argue that: (i) the RPD misapprehended evidence that it had cited from the National Documentation Package ("NDP") regarding the Nigerian police reports; and (ii) the RPD erred in making an erroneous plausibility finding. Manner in which police reports were obtained is not credible and contradictory of objective NDP evidence

The RPD found that the police reports were not reliable and could not be afforded any evidentiary weight for a number of reasons, one such reason being that the process by which the Appellants alleged they were obtained differed materially from information contained in the NDP.13 The Appellants allege that the RPD failed to meaningfully engage with the NDP and, as a result, grossly misapprehended the evidence and that the police reports were obtained by a relative in Nigeria at their behest after they had arrived in Canada. Specifically, as testified by the Principal Appellant: "I asked him to go to the police station where we reported the case. And he went there and that was where they gave it to him."14 It would appear that no authorization letter or affidavit was provided to this relative to facilitate obtaining the police reports.

In making this finding, the RPD relied upon information from the NDP which indicates that: (i) police reports can be obtained by a third party provided that the person to whom the documents were initially issued authorizes that third party to obtain a copy; 15 (ii) when specifically asked about obtaining a police report from abroad, a law associate indicated that a police report cannot be obtained "in absentia";16 and (iii) the "affidavit must be deposed by the person who has direct knowledge of the content of the affidavit and not a third party."17 The comment referenced at item (iii) above was made specifically with respect to allegations of stolen goods or missing property. While the allegations made by the Appellants are much more encompassing than stolen property, there is that element to the claim since they allege that the men who broke into their house stole laptops and cellphones.

The Appellants argue that the portion of the NDP indicating that a police report cannot be obtained "in absentia" references the submission of a complaint to police for the first time which requires an affidavit to be deposed by someone with first hand knowledge of the matter reported.18 I disagree with this interpretation of the NDP. By reading this Response to Information Request excerpt in a contextual manner, I am of the view that the proper interpretation is that when requesting a copy or copies of police reports from abroad, someone must attend the police station in person. If the person who attends the police station has no direct knowledge of the incident, he or she must present themselves armed with an affidavit (in the event the report deals with stolen goods or missing property) or some form of authorization from the party who does have direct knowledge of the incident. I note that on the issue of authorization, the Appellants indicate in their memorandum, "...the only thing he needed to do was authorize his brother-in-law to collect the copies on his behalf, which presumably he did"19 [emphasis added]. With respect to counsel, the evidentiary record does not support the notion that the Principal Appellant provided his brother-in-law with an affidavit in prescribed form or a letter of authorization, and I do not accept counsel's presumption as compelling or persuasive. I note that the Appellants have had ample opportunity to submit such evidence, if it existed, since the RPD decision was rendered and to have it considered for admission as new evidence and have failed to do so.

Moreover, to accept counsel's argument that it is only applicable where a report is being made in the first instance means that there would be no police report to obtain, in absentia or otherwise, because the incident would not have been reported as yet. As such, I agree with and confirm the RPD finding that the Principal Appellant's testimony regarding the manner by which the police reports were obtained conflicts with the objective NDP evidence. This undermines the Appellants' credibility and, as the police reports allegedly involve the reporting of, one of the most significant incidents of alleged persecutory conduct, this finding also undermines the credibility of the claim. Uncontested credibility findings

The RPD made several adverse credibility findings which appear to be uncontested. Examples of such findings are as follows: (i) the Principal Appellant's failure to produce the XXXX XXXX or to have requested a copy of it from his former employer; (ii) the Principal Appellant's failure to conduct any sort of follow up with police or to make enquiries as to the status of the XXXX XXXX - in fact, he did not even "Google" the incident on the internet to determine its status; (iii) certain "chat" messages tendered on the day of the hearing purportedly to establish attempts to secure corroborative documents from Nigeria were found by the RPD to have likely been fabricated to buttress the Appellants' account and were, therefore, unreliable; (iv) various affidavits were filled with information that likely originated with the Appellants and were not relating to first-hand knowledge of the affiants, in such a way that they were not found to be reliable and were not given any weight; and (v) the XXXX report of XXXX XXXX, received no weight owing to the degree upon which it relied on the self-report of the Principal Appellant whose account of the allegations was, on a balance of probabilities, not credible. The fact that these negative credibility findings are uncontested impact the claim significantly across a broad range of allegations ranging from the police investigation to attempts to obtain corroborative documents to the self-reported impact of the alleged persecutory conduct which cannot be disregarded or ignored as they have clearly impact upon the credibility of the claim.

I might add that the IRB transcript discloses other aspects of the Appellants' testimony not included in the RPD decision but which warrant mention in my determination, as they also impact upon the credibility of the Principal Appellant's testimony. When questioned by the RPD about the process by which the family obtained their USA visas, the Principal Appellant testified that it had been handled by an agent and that he had not reviewed the visa applications before they were submitted. Previously, he had testified that the visa application had showed him as working at XXXX XXXX.20 When asked how he knew the application form correctly identified his employer if he had never reviewed the application, the Principal Appellant provides the following evasive and non-responsive answer which speculates as to what he might have done: No, because before I applied for the visa I must have got a letter of introduction from the XXXX to do that. That's why I'm sure that he can't - I want to believe that he couldn't have put anything (inaudible) because U.S. Consulate, they will ask for a letter from my office which I must have submitted before the application was processed.21

Similarly, the neighbour's affidavit provides enriched detail with respect to allegations regarding the incident where the Appellants allege that three armed men entered their residence, slapped the Principal Appellant and forced the other Appellants to lie facedown on the floor while they stole laptops and cellphones. While the neighbour's affidavit refers to himself as the Minor Appellants' "personal home lesson teacher"22 and indicates that he was at the residence giving them a home lesson,23 the Principal Appellant's testimony makes no reference of the neighbour's presence, specifically referencing that the armed men "asked us to lie down flat, my wife and my children."24 Neither the Appellants' Basis of Claim nor the Principal Appellants' testimony mentions the fact that the neighbour was present, an omission which I find to be material and impacts upon credibility. I am of the view that it would be reasonable to expect, if credible, that the neighbour's account of the incident and the Principal Appellant's account of the same incident, particularly with respect to the fact that an eyewitness may have been present at the time, would have been in alignment. Instead the inconsistency creates further credibility concerns regarding the Appellants' supporting document, the Principal Appellant's testimony and the credibility of the claim.

As indicated, while these items were not featured in the RPD decision, nor was it argued in the Appellant's memorandum, I am of the view that it does not constitute a new issue requiring notice to the Appellants. Although I cannot raise a new issue without putting the parties on notice, I am entitled to make independent findings of credibility where credibility was (as is the case herein) an issue before the RPD and where the finding derives from the evidentiary record.25 Moreover, the Federal Court in Sary states as follows: The situation is quite different in this case. The RAD did not raise a "new issue" by pointing out the contradiction between Mr. XXXX visa application and his testimony on how he found his job in TroisRivières. It simply made reference to another piece of evidence in the tribunal's file which supported the RPD's findings on Mr. XXXX lack of credibility. The RPD's decision and Mr. XXXX submissions dealt extensively with this credibility issue and the arguments in its regard. This is not a situation where the decision maker considered extrinsic evidence without giving Mr. XXXX the opportunity to review it. On the contrary, Mr. XXXX credibility constituted the very basis of the RPD's decision and the appeal filed by Mr. XXXX.26

In this regard, the Principal Appellant provided questionable and unreliable testimony with respect to both the Appellants' US visa application and what is perhaps the most significant persecutory event alleged; accordingly, I draw a negative inference with respect to his credibility. The RPD erred with respect to implausibility finding, but such error fails to impact upon determination

The RPD found it implausible that only the Principal Appellant was targeted as a result of the investigation into the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Appellants argue that implausibility findings should only be made in the clearest of circumstances. Based upon my review of the evidence and in light of the jurisprudence,27 I agree that it is an implausibility finding one which I am not at all certain is solidly grounded in the "clearest of circumstances." In this regard, I agree with the Appellants that the implausibility finding is not supported by the evidence, however, in light of the multiple credibility issues discussed above, it does not impact upon my ultimate decision.

Regardless of my finding that the RPD erred in the implausibility finding regarding the Principal Appellant (and his family) being the sole targets of the agents of persecution, as a result of a number of credibility issues - both uncontested and contested - the Appellants have failed to credibly establish, on a balance of probabilities, the allegations of bank fraud and the participation of the agents of persecution, not to mention the persecutory actions which they claim followed. As a result, I find that on a forward-looking basis, the Appellants have not established that, if returned to Nigeria, they face a serious possibility of persecution based on a Convention ground, nor have they established, on a balance of probabilities, that they are persons in need of protection. As such, the appeal must necessarily fail.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
